text.title: Node.js Service Layer Implementation Core Rules
text.summary: Seven rules for the TypeScript Express + Prisma implementation: where untrusted input becomes a typed value, how a rejected promise reaches the error middleware, the four-argument signature that makes a handler an error handler, which Prisma error codes map to which status, and what each layer's tests are allowed to touch.

rule.statement: Every controller parses `req.body`, `req.query` and `req.params` through a schema (`schema.parse(...)` with Zod or equivalent) before use, and the service method signature takes the inferred type (`z.infer<typeof CreateOrderInput>`). No service parameter may be typed `any`, `Request`, or an index-signature object.

rationale.source: @types/express — Request.body is typed `any`; Zod documentation on inference

rule.rationale: Under `@types/express` `req.body` is `any`, so `strict: true` gives exactly zero protection at the one place untrusted data enters the process — a typo in a field name compiles fine and reaches the database as `undefined`. A single `parse` call is where the static type first becomes a checked claim.

rule.statement: On Express 4 every async route handler MUST be wrapped (`catchAsync(fn)` or `express-async-handler`); a bare `async (req, res) => ...` registered on a router is rejected. On Express 5 the wrapper is unnecessary and the artefact MUST state which major version is in use.

rationale.source: Express 5 migration guide — 'rejected promises from middleware and handlers are forwarded to next(err)'

rule.rationale: Express 4 ignores the returned promise, so a rejection never reaches `next()`. The response is never written, the client hangs until its own timeout, and the only trace is an `unhandledRejection` — which under Node 15+ terminates the process by default, so one bad row restarts the server.

rule.statement: The terminal error handler MUST be declared with exactly four parameters `(err, req, res, next)`, registered after all routes and routers, and MUST NOT include `err.stack` or `err.message` from an unmapped error in the response body when NODE_ENV is production.

rationale.source: Express documentation — Error Handling ('error-handling middleware is identified by four arguments')

rule.rationale: Express selects error middleware by function arity. Drop the unused `next` and the function is registered as ordinary middleware: it never runs on error, errors fall through to the default handler, and the default handler returns the stack trace to the caller in development-like configurations.

rule.statement: Repositories catch `Prisma.PrismaClientKnownRequestError` and translate at minimum P2002 (unique constraint) to ConflictError, P2025 (record required but not found) to NotFoundError, and P2003 (foreign key constraint) to ValidationError. No raw Prisma error object may propagate past a repository.

rationale.source: Prisma documentation — error reference P2002 / P2003 / P2025

rule.rationale: An unmapped known-request error is caught by the generic branch of the error middleware and returned as 500, so a duplicate email — a client mistake with a correct 409 answer — is reported as a server fault and retried by the client. Its `meta.target` also names the table and columns, which the 500 body then discloses.

rule.statement: Service unit tests inject an in-memory object implementing the repository interface — no database, no `jest.mock('@prisma/client')`. Query correctness is covered separately by repository tests against a real PostgreSQL instance, each worker on its own schema or its own container.

rationale.source: Meszaros, xUnit Test Patterns — Test Double vs mocking the collaborator's API

rule.rationale: Mocking the Prisma client asserts on the arguments you passed, so a `where` clause with the wrong field passes every service test and fails only in production. Sharing one database across Jest workers is the other half: parallel truncations delete rows another worker is mid-assertion on, which reads as flakiness rather than as a fixture bug.

rule.statement: `tsconfig.json` sets `strict: true`, and ESLint runs the type-aware rules `@typescript-eslint/no-floating-promises` and `no-misused-promises` with `parserOptions.project` pointing at that tsconfig. The lint step runs in CI, not only in the editor.

rationale.source: typescript-eslint documentation — no-floating-promises requires type information

rule.rationale: TypeScript itself accepts a discarded promise. An un-awaited repository call inside a `$transaction` callback lets the callback resolve first, so the transaction commits or rolls back before the write is issued — and whether the row lands depends on event-loop timing, which is why it survives review and CI without this rule.

rule.statement: Skip when the architecture artefact from nodejs-service-layer-architecture does not exist or is unapproved, or when the stack is plain JavaScript with no TypeScript migration agreed — six of the seven rules above are type-system or Prisma-specific and degrade to unenforceable advice. Emit a structured skip naming the missing precondition.
rule.rationale: Implementing layers before the layer decisions are settled produces code that has to be moved once the boundaries are chosen, and the move is what silently drops the transaction ownership rule.
